Besides osteoarthritis, also other joint pathologies of the knee can be causative for a Baker's cyst.  Radiotherapy is known to be an effective treatment for osteoarthritis, with an anti-inflammatory effect.  As the excessive production of synovia usually is associated with intraarticular inflammation, our hypothesis was that radiotherapy might positively influence the synovial production and reduce the volume of a Baker's cyst.  Materials and methods: We performed a prospective trial, including 20 knees receiving radiotherapy for knee arthritis.  Besides documentation of NRS (numeric rating scale), WOMAC (Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index) score and Knee Society Score, the volume of the Baker's cyst was calculated for a short- (6 to 12 weeks) and long-term (9 to 12 months) follow-up.  Ultrasonic volumetry was performed using an ultrasound device with a high-resolution multifrequency linear probe (6-9 MHz).  Results: Low-dose radiotherapy improved NRS, WOMAC score and Knee Society Score significantly.  The mean volume of Baker's cyst decreased from 22.3 ml to 10.7 respectively 3.1 ml during follow-up. Conclusion: Radiotherapy of knee osteoarthritis is an effective treatment that decreases the volume of a Baker's cyst.  Most patients respond to the treatment.  Whether radiotherapy is an effective treatment for Baker's cyst without associated osteoarthritis has to be further examined.

Methods: Forty-two consecutive patients with symptomatic popliteal cysts received arthroscopic treatment. According to the MRI results, the cyst disappeared in 11 (55%), shrank in size in 6 (30%) and existed in 3 (15%) patients in the AI group, and was absent in 18 (81.8%) and shrank in size in 4 (18.2%) patients in the AICR group, suggesting a significant difference between the two (P < 0.05). Conclusion: Additional resection of cyst wall can result in a lower recurrence rate of cysts but extend the operation time and increase the incidence of perioperative complications compared with arthroscopic internal drainage of popliteal cysts alone.

# Understanding Airway Sensitivity and Asthma

Your airways can become too sensitive. This is called bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR). It is the main condition that leads to asthma.

## What Makes Airways More Sensitive

Your airways can become more sensitive from things inside your body or from things outside your body. Weather and climate can also affect them. When your airways get inflamed, they become more sensitive. Swelling in the airways makes the problem worse.

## Common Asthma Triggers

These things can trigger asthma in people who are at risk:
- Viral infections in your upper airways
- Allergens (things you are allergic to)
- Long-term swelling in your upper airways
- Things that irritate your airways
- Some pain medicines

## How to Treat Airway Sensitivity

Doctors can treat this condition with steroid and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs. Living near the ocean may also help improve airway sensitivity. Ocean air may reduce irritants like allergens. It may also work in other ways.

## Weather Effects on Asthma

Cold weather fronts and high wind speeds can make asthma worse. Living near the Baltic sea area improved airway sensitivity in some patients.

## Future Research

Doctors are starting new studies. These studies will look at preventing asthma in people at high risk. The studies will test whether living near the ocean really helps asthma patients.
